The archive accessible through today's page also stores previous days' solutions. Comparing past targets and their corresponding answers reveals patterns in difficulty. Some days favor muted midtones; others push toward saturated primaries or near-blacks. Knowing what the typical distribution looks like helps calibrate expectations when you're staring at an unfamiliar hue.

Why additive color logic beats random mixing

Players coming from art backgrounds often struggle initially because they apply subtractive color thinking. Pigment mixing works oppositely—adding colors makes things darker. Additive mixing flips that: combining red, green, and blue light at full intensity produces white, not muddy brown.

This distinction explains why some guesses look promising on screen but score poorly. You might see a grayish result and assume you're close, but if that gray comes from unbalanced channels, the algorithm registers significant drift. True proximity means each channel lands within a tight tolerance of its target value, not just the visual appearance matching roughly.

When adjusting after a miss, resist the urge to flip channels wildly. Small nudges—dropping a channel by 10-20 points while raising another—typically yield better results than overhauling everything. The color space doesn't reward dramatic swings; it rewards precision.

From there, adjust one channel at a time. Raise red if the target feels too cyan-green. Lower green if it skews yellow. Watch how the feedback widget moves with each tweak. Within two or three calibrated adjustments, most players land within acceptable range.

The hint system on this page offers directional cues if you're truly lost. Use those sparingly—they narrow possibilities but don't hand over the exact numbers. Treat hints as training wheels, not crutches.

The standard input field accepts 0-255 integer ranges per channel. Converting percentages to that scale is simple: multiply your percentage by 2.55 and round to the nearest whole number. Most players find the integer scale intuitive once they've mixed a few rounds.

The target color sits at the top of the board, and three input slots wait below. Each slot accepts a red-green-blue value ranging from 0 to 255. When combined additively, these three colors stack to produce the answer shown on today's card. Reading the mix correctly means treating this as a light-mixing problem, not a paint problem. What the source colors are telling you

A careful player examines the revealed portion of each source slot before committing to a guess. The brightness of each channel matters more than the hue alone. For example, a high red value (200+) paired with low green and blue suggests warmth dominating the final mix. Watching which channels spike across your three guesses reveals whether you're overshooting or undershooting the target.

Some players miss the obvious: the target itself gives feedback. After each guess, the board shows how close you came. That gap between your result and the target tells you exactly which channel needs adjustment. A bluish result means you pushed blue too hard. Dial it back and compensate elsewhere.

Why additive color logic beats random mixing

Randomly cycling through RGB values hoping to stumble onto the answer wastes guesses. Additive color mixing follows predictable rules. Red plus green equals yellow. Green plus blue equals cyan. Blue plus red equals magenta. All three at full intensity produce white. This triangle of relationships narrows your search space dramatically.

The mistake most new players make is thinking in terms of paint or ink. Subtractive mixing (what happens when you blend pigments) produces muddy browns when you over-combine colors. Additive mixing does the opposite—adding more light makes things brighter, not dirtier. Keep this distinction clear and your guess efficiency improves immediately.

Easy adjustment path for the next Colorfle

If today's puzzle didn't click, here's what works: start with equal RGB values to land near grayscale, then adjust one channel at a time. This isolates cause and effect. Once you know which direction a channel needs to move, fine-tune in increments of 20-30 rather than guessing wildly.

The archive link on this page lets you review past puzzles and see how solutions varied. Some days the target skews warm; others favor cool tones. Building familiarity with typical target distributions trains your eye for faster initial guesses.

Questions players keep asking

Does the order of my three colors matter?

No. Additive mixing is commutative—red+green+blue produces the same result regardless of sequence. What matters is getting each channel's total value correct.

Can I reuse the same color in multiple slots?

Yes, there's no rule preventing duplicate entries. Using the same color twice simply doubles its contribution to that channel. This sometimes helps when you need a very specific channel balance.

What's the fastest way to improve from multiple wrong guesses?

After each incorrect attempt, identify your worst-performing channel (the one furthest from the target's corresponding value). Focus your next guess entirely on correcting that single channel while holding the others steady. This binary-search approach converges faster than scattered adjustments.

Are there standard reference points I should memorize?

Knowing a few anchor combinations helps: pure white is 255/255/255, black is 0/0/0, and the secondary colors sit at 255/255/0 (yellow), 0/255/255 (cyan), and 255/0/255 (magenta). From there, you can interpolate toward any intermediate target.

How do I handle a target that's mostly one color?

When the target leans heavily toward one channel, consider allocating two of your three slots to that dominant color. For instance, a predominantly red target might use red twice with small green and blue contributions. This isn't always necessary, but it often reduces the number of adjustment cycles needed.
